data.title: Supreme Court upholds Karnataka HC order lifting ban on bike taxis
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed the Karnataka government's appeal against the Karnataka High Court's decision to allow bike taxi services to operate in the state.
 
A Bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N Kotiswar Singh passed the order, upholding the high court's January 23 judgment that lifted the ban on bike taxis and allowed operators to apply for permits to run the services, Bar and Bench reported.
 

What did the Karnataka High Court ruling say?

 
In its January order, the high court ruled that motorcycles could be registered as transport vehicles and operated as contract carriages under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. It held that the state government could impose regulatory conditions but could not refuse permits solely on the ground that the vehicles were two-wheelers.
 
 
A division bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice CM Joshi allowed appeals filed by ANI Technologies, which operates Ola, alongside Uber Rapido, motorcycle owners and the Bike Taxi Welfare Association. The appeals challenged an earlier order that barred bike taxi operations until the state framed a policy. 
ALSO READ: UP amends tourism policy to promote budget hotels, homestays and rest stops
 
The high court directed transport authorities to consider applications to register motorcycles as transport vehicles and grant contract carriage permits. It also allowed authorities to impose necessary operational conditions.
 

Why Karnataka govt appealed against the high court order?

 
Karnataka banned bike taxi services in March 2024, citing concerns over passenger safety, alleged misuse of the existing policy and the absence of electric two-wheelers on ride-hailing platforms.
 
The state later challenged the high court's ruling in the Supreme Court, citing passenger safety and insurance coverage concerns. Five auto and taxi driver associations also challenged the decision, arguing that allowing bike taxis without comparable regulatory obligations would adversely affect existing transport operators.
 
Bike taxi services operated by aggregators such as Ola, Uber and Rapido will continue to operate in Karnataka.

data.title: HDFC Bank regains ₹13 trillion market-cap; stock hits 8-month high
data.description:
HDFC Bank share price movement

 
HDFC Bank on Friday regained ₹13 trillion market capitalisation (market cap) as the stock price of the private sector giant hit an eight-month high of ₹846.60, surging 3 per cent on the BSE in intraday deals. 
 
HDFC Bank’s share price surpassed its previous high of ₹842.15 touched on July 7, 2026. It quoted at its highest level since March 18, 2026. The stock hit a 52-week high of ₹1,017.90 on December 1, 2025.
 
Thus far in November 2026, HDFC Bank outperformed the market by surging 22 per cent, as compared to a 12.4 per cent rise in the BSE Sensex.
 
 
HDFC Bank’s market cap hit ₹13.06 trillion in intraday deals, surpassing recently-listed Reliance Group Company Jio Platforms (₹12.8 trillion market cap). 
 
Currently, HDFC Bank stood at the third position in the overall market cap ranking of BSE-listed companies. Reliance Industries tops the list, with ₹ 18.40 trillion market cap followed by Bharti Airtel at ₹13.47 trillion market cap. Check - TOP GAINERS NSE | TOP LOSERS NSE
 

What’s driving HDFC Bank’s stock price in November?

 
HDFC Bank is a leading private sector bank with consistent growth and operational performance across various cycles. Post-merger, the bank has become the second largest in terms of size with a diversified portfolio. HDFC Bank is the largest private sector bank with a loan book of ₹31 trillion.
 
Meanwhile, the Nifty Bank index hit a new all-time high of 64,450, gaining 2.2 per cent on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) in Friday’s intraday deals, surging 4 per cent in the past two trading days. The sharp rally in private and public sector banks (PSBs) is aided by strong buying from foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). Thus far in November, the Nifty Bank index outperformed the market by soaring 17.8 per cent, as compared to a 11.7 per cent rally in the Nifty 50.
 
According to the National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) data, FPIs net bought a record number of shares worth ₹1.15 trillion ($12.21 trillion) in November.
 
Meanwhile, HDFC Bank appears to be nearing an inflection point, with September 2026 quarter (Q2) margins at a trough, improving operating productivity, and accelerating retail/micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) momentum setting the stage for a gradual recovery in earnings.
 
The higher share of floating rate loans, along with an improving mix of better-yielding Retail/MSME loans and focused efforts to mobilise current account saving account (CASA) deposits, bode well from a margins standpoint. The appointment of Anup Bagchi as MD & CEO addresses the leadership overhang; however, his strategic direction, particularly on retail growth, deposit mobilisation and NIM improvement, will be key to sustaining the bank’s re-rating, the brokerage firm said in the Q2 result update. 
ALSO READ: Sensex zooms 1790 pts in 2 days; ₹6.9 trn added to m-cap: 5 key reasons
 
Analysts at Axis Securities remain constructive on HDFC Bank's medium-term growth outlook, supported by improving branch productivity, a gradual recovery in retail credit growth, a strengthening liability franchise and best-in-class asset quality. The brokerage firm expects return on asset (RoA) to improve to 1.8-1.9 per cent over FY27-29E.  Analysts believe the risk-reward remains favourable, and with most risks largely addressed, the downside on the stock appears limited. The brokerage has a ‘Buy’ rating on HDFC Bank with a target price of ₹950 per share.
 
“We expect RoA to remain around 1.8 per cent over FY27–28E, supported by gradual margin recovery, benign credit cost and improving operating efficiency. Stepping down of Kaizad, DMD, brings in near term uncertainty. Anup Bagchi’s appointment as MD & CEO marks a key leadership transition, with his forthcoming strategy on growth, margins and balance sheet optimisation remains awaited,” analysts at ICICI Securities said in the result update. Factoring all, the brokerage firm said it continues to value standalone bank at ~1.8x FY28E book value and ₹118 for subsidiaries, thus keeping target unchanged at ₹925. The brokerage maintains a 'Buy' rating on the stock. ALSO READ: Airtel overtakes HDFC Bank to become India's most valuable brand: Report Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion.

data.title: SpiceJet's ₹5,500-cr fundraise: Can it revive the airline's operations?
data.description:
Low-cost carrier SpiceJet is planning to raise up to ₹5,500 crore amid mounting payment disputes, grounded aircraft and a sharp loss of market share. This is the latest attempt by the airline which has underwent several fundraising and revival attempts over the years.
 
The airline's immediate operational difficulties show the scale of the challenge. SpiceJet cancelled 31 of its 42 scheduled flights at Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru airports on Thursday. The cancellations came amid a cash crunch and mounting dues to service providers and aircraft lessors.
 
The proposed fundraising, approved by the airline's board earlier this week, could involve equity and other permitted financial instruments. SpiceJet said the proceeds would help ease liquidity pressures, strengthen its balance sheet, restore flights, support fleet expansion and meet operational requirements. The airline is also in discussions with potential investors, news agency Reuters reported.
 

Market share falls as operations shrink

The scale of SpiceJet's decline is evident in its passenger numbers. Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) data show that its domestic market share fell from 3.9 per cent in January 2026 to 0.6 per cent in September. Its passenger numbers declined from 592,000 to just 73,000 during the same period.
 
The September figures also placed SpiceJet below regional carrier Star Air, which had a 0.7 per cent market share.
 
 
The airline recorded a cancellation rate of 20.29 per cent during the month, the highest among scheduled domestic carriers, according to the DGCA.
 
Financial uncertainty has also added to the pressure. SpiceJet has not filed its financial results for the March and June 2026 quarters. The airline attributed the delay to the time required to complete the audit, Reuters reported. The Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) has warned that trading in its shares could be suspended from December 10 if the results are not submitted by December 7.
 
The airline's cash constraints have also affected aircraft availability. The Times of India reported that six recently leased aircraft remained grounded over unpaid dues to lessors. Moldova-based FLYONE, a privately owned low-cost airline, also terminated an agreement to lease three aircraft to SpiceJet over outstanding payments.

When did the crisis begin?

SpiceJet's financial troubles are not new. Its FY15 annual report traced the crisis to delayed funding, legacy liabilities and mounting payment obligations to service providers, aircraft lessors and banks.
 
The airline said the non-receipt of expected funding at the beginning of FY15 weakened its cash position, leading to defaults on payments to tax authorities, employees, airport operators, suppliers and other creditors.
 
The defaults resulted in the return of multiple aircraft to lessors and flight cancellations. SpiceJet's average daily flights fell from 340 in July 2014 to 230 in December 2014, reducing revenue.
 
The situation worsened after the DGCA imposed restrictions on forward bookings, cancelled slots and increased safety surveillance in December 2014. SpiceJet's annual report said these regulatory measures led to an immediate decline of about 90 per cent in cash inflows. The airline partially suspended operations in mid-December.
 
In January 2015, the board approved a revival plan under which Ajay Singh took over management and control from the previous promoters, Kalanithi Maran and Kal Airways.
 

The 2024 fundraise brought temporary relief

The airline continued to face financial difficulties in subsequent years, with losses and legal disputes over unpaid dues to aircraft lessors, lenders and other creditors.
 
In September 2024, SpiceJet raised ₹3,000 crore through a qualified institutional placement (QIP). The promoter group also infused ₹500 crore during FY25, including a final tranche of ₹294.09 crore.
 
The airline's FY25 annual report said ₹2,699.54 crore of the QIP proceeds had been utilised by March 31, 2025. The funds went towards statutory dues, creditor settlements, aircraft maintenance and ungrounding, fleet induction, employee-related payments and airport dues.
 
The capital infusion coincided with an improvement in financial performance. SpiceJet reported a standalone profit after tax of ₹58.07 crore in FY25, against a loss of ₹409.44 crore in FY24. Its net worth also turned positive at ₹683.02 crore as of March 31, 2025, compared with a negative ₹2,585.85 crore a year earlier.
 
However, the improvement did not resolve its underlying financial problems. The airline's FY25 annual report recorded accumulated losses of ₹7,764.81 crore and a deficit of ₹3,845.07 crore between current assets and current liabilities. Its statutory auditors also flagged a material uncertainty related to the company's ability to continue as a going concern.

Grounded aircraft deepen the financial strain

Aircraft availability remains central to SpiceJet's difficulties. Its FY25 annual report said a large part of its fleet had become non-operational because of maintenance-related issues. It added that aircraft underutilisation had affected profitability, while payments to lessors, vendors and statutory authorities had been deferred.
 
CARE Ratings' assessment published in April 2026 gave a longer-term picture of the decline.
 
SpiceJet's operating fleet fell from 114 aircraft in March 2020 to 25 in March 2025, before recovering to 33 in December 2025. However, around 37 aircraft remained grounded at the time of the assessment, with the rating agency citing unpaid lessor dues, financial constraints and shortages of components and spare parts.
 
CARE downgraded the airline's long-term bank facility rating to CARE B+ from CARE BB-, citing its deteriorating financial risk profile and stretched liquidity. It also identified the low number of operational aircraft and operating losses as factors affecting performance.
 
The operational and financial problems reinforce each other. Cash shortages and unpaid dues make it harder to maintain aircraft, settle lessor payments and bring grounded planes back into service. A smaller operational fleet restricts flight capacity, limiting the airline's ability to carry passengers and generate revenue. The resulting pressure on earnings and cash flows makes it harder to fund maintenance and expand operations.

Can another fundraise change the trajectory?

The proposed ₹5,500-crore fundraise comes after the ₹3,000-crore QIP in 2024 and the improvement in FY25 results. But the latest decline in market share, delayed financial filings and aircraft-related payment disputes show that the earlier capital infusion has not delivered a sustained operational recovery.
 
The board's approval of the ₹5,500-crore fundraise is subject to the necessary shareholder and regulatory approvals.
 
The extent to which the fundraise improves SpiceJet's financial position and operational capacity will become clearer from its ability to mobilise the funds, bring grounded aircraft back into service and increase flight operations.

data.title: India VIX up 9%, tops 17-mark; analysts say FII flows keep bulls in control
data.description:
India VIX, the volatility gauge of the domestic equity market, climbed nearly 9 per cent on Friday, signalling heightened uncertainty among traders even as benchmark indices extended their gains.
 
As of 1:30 PM, India VIX was up 8.8 per cent at 17.53. The benchmark Nifty 50 rose 185 points, or 0.72 per cent, to 25,700, while the BSE Sensex gained 630 points, or 0.76 per cent, to trade at 83,655.
 
Notably, India VIX has risen for the third consecutive session, gaining over 12 per cent during the period. The rise in volatility has come even as the Nifty 50 advanced more than 300 points, or 1.2 per cent, over the same period.
 
 
India VIX indicates expected volatility in the market over the next 30 days. A sustained rise in India VIX generally indicates increasing expectations of larger market swings and often coincides with cautious investor sentiment. It can also lead to higher option premiums.  Analysts said that the sharp 12 per cent  rise in India VIX over the last three sessions indicates increasing nervousness and uncertainty among market participants, with traders increasingly seeking protection against potential volatility.  "This is particularly significant as the Nifty is trading less than 3% away from its all-time high, suggesting that caution is building despite the broader positive market structure. However, a rise in VIX does not necessarily indicate an imminent correction; rather, it signals expectations of larger market swings over the coming weeks," Sudeep Shah, head - technical and derivatives research at SBI Securities, said. At today's high of 25,745.75, data showed that the Nifty 50 index is less than 3 per cent away from the record high of 26,373.20, touched on January 5, 2026.  READ MORE: Sensex zooms 1790 pts in 2 days; ₹6.9 trn added to m-cap: 5 reasons
 
From a technical perspective, Harish Jujarey, AVP, head - technical equity research, Prithvi Finmart, said that India VIX has moved above its key 50 & 200 - day moving averages, indicating a shift towards a higher volatility moves.  
 
"Going ahead, 18.50 will be an immediate resistance level. A decisive move above this could push India VIX towards the higher range of 27–28, signalling heightened volatility in the equity market," he said. FIIs power market rally 
Analysts said that profit booking is happening in the market but the FII buying is so sustained and aggressive that the bulls are calling the shots. Despite occasional dips, the market is likely to remain resilient on the back of massive FII flows assisted by impressive corporate earnings. 
 
VK Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist, Geojit Investments, said that weakening of the AI trade continues with another 2.25 per cent cut in Nasdaq yesterday, and this is dragging other AI-related markets like South Korea, Taiwan and Japan down. Nifty is the only high performing market in the world this month with a 10.7 per cent surge in just 13 trading days.
 
"It is important to note that the bulk of the FII flows have gone into financial services, particularly the banking majors. FIIs are now buying the very same stocks they have been selling to raise money for the AI trade. Telecom also has been attracting big inflows. The sharp correction in metal prices have attracted buying in auto stocks and consumer durables," he said. FIIs buying this week
 
According to exchange data, foreign institutional investors (FIIs) remained net buyers of Indian equities on all four trading days this week. They purchased shares worth ₹4,864.68 crore on Monday, ₹4,195.38 crore on Tuesday, ₹5,866.78 crore on Wednesday and ₹7,411.41 crore on Thursday. 'Avoid aggressive fresh buying' 
Meanwhile, Sudeep suggested investors to avoid aggressive fresh buying in Nifty at elevated levels, and adopt a staggered investment approach and remain selective, as some consolidation near record highs would be healthy for the market.
 
"Investors should closely monitor Nifty's key support levels, FII activity, global market cues, crude oil prices and overall market breadth. A sustained rise in VIX alongside weakening market breadth and a breach of important support levels could trigger profit booking," he said.

data.title: PMO adviser flags discom hurdles in expanding India's EV charging network
data.description:
Tarun Kapoor, advisor to the Prime Minister, on Friday flagged lack of cooperation from electricity distribution companies in scaling the electric vehicle charging network in the country.

He also said the government is open to additional funding for the charging infrastructure if required.

"DISCOMs sometimes are not very cooperative," Kapoor said while speaking at the SIAM's first Growth and Readiness for EV Infrastructure Dialogue on Friday.

According to him, distribution companies sometimes demand a substantial amount when setting up charging stations, particularly high capacity ones, and there is a need for a dedicated officer in every distribution company to address this issue.

"The cost of putting up a charging station as you all know the higher part of the cost is behind the metre where sometimes the distribution companies demand a huge amount of money," he said.

 

"Particularly if the charging station needs a higher capacity, say going to 100 KW or more then sometimes they ask for quite a huge amount of money." Kapoor noted that electric vehicles will be an important future source of electricity demand, creating a significant business opportunity for power distribution companies.

"We have been telling DISCOMs that now time has come to realise that EV is going to become one of their largest sectors for power consumption. And as a country we are entering a phase where there is surplus power available," he said.

Kapoor said the government is looking to encourage daytime charging rather than relying completely on overnight charging at homes. Charging facilities should increasingly be located at offices, workplaces, marketplaces and parking areas.

However, low utilisation at some of the existing public charging stations is also a concern, which impacts their maintenance and long-term viability.

Kapoor said some charging stations had utilisation levels of less than 1 per cent, making maintenance difficult for operators.

Adoption of electric vehicles in India is at an early stage, with faster adoption seen in two and three-wheeler segments. Charging infrastructure is one of the key bottlenecks to wider adoption.

Under the Rs 11,900 crore PM E-Drive scheme, the government has set aside Rs 2,000 crore to subsidise charging infrastructure, including up to 72,300 new public EV charging stations, battery swapping stations, and battery charging stations.

"There is a good amount of money available going forward to establish charging infrastructure. And I think the government would be willing to put in more funds also if need be," he added.

data.title: Sensex zooms 1790 pts in 2 days; ₹6.9 trn added to m-cap: 5 key reasons
data.description:
The Indian benchmark indices are on a winning streak as they gained nearly 1 per cent in Friday's intraday session, extending rise to the second day. Meanwhile, they have risen in four of the five trading sessions this week.
 
In intraday deals, 30-pack Sensex added 803 points or 0.97 per cent to hit the day's high of 83,825. In last trade, it gained 990 points, taking the two-day rise to 1,793 points or 2.2 per cent.
 
Similarly, its NSE counterpart Nifty 50 gained 231 points or 0.90 per cent during the day to rise to the day's peak of 25,746. In a span of two days it has gained 518 points or 2.05 per cent.
 
 
During this period, the market capitalisation of BSE-listed stocks has increased by ₹6.90 trillion from ₹506.47 trillion on Wednesday to ₹513.37 trillion today.  
 
Both the benchmark indices are now less than 3 per cent from reclaiming their all-time high levels. The sharp nearly 12 per cent rise seen in November has helped them rebound after a prolonged phase of consolidation.
 

What's driving Indian stock markets?

Here are key factors behind the rise in the Sensex and Nifty today:
 
1. Bank stocks rally
Index-heavyweight banks and financials emerged as the top contributors to the rise seen in the flagship indices today. HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Kotak Bank and Axis Bank alone contributed over 500 points or nearly 65 per cent gains seen in the Sensex today.   
ALSO READ: Stock Market LIVE: Sensex jumps 700 pts, Nifty above 25,700; Meesho hits new high
 
The sharp rally in leading private bank stocks has also driven the Nifty Bank above the 64,000 mark for the first time. Data for the first fortnight of November shows that financial services attracted the bulk of the FII inflows at ₹43,102 crore.
 
FIIs are now buying the very same stocks they have been selling to raise money for the AI trade, said Dr VK Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist, Geojit Investment.
 
2. FPI buying
November has seen record buying from foreign investors, with NSDL showing net inflows of 1.14 trillion - the highest ever in a month till date. Strong FPI interest has been a major driver for the Indian equity market, especially as they pivot away from AI-related bets in global markets.
 
"FII buying is so sustained and aggressive that the bulls are calling the shots. Despite occasional dips, the market is likely to remain resilient on the back of massive FII flows assisted by impressive corporate earnings," said Vijayakumar.
 
3. Oil weakness
The oil prices are set for a weekly decline even as they eked out minor gains today. Lower crude oil prices bode well for import-focussed economies like India as it improves the macroeconomic outlook and strengthens the current account deficit.
 
Currently, oil prices are hovering around $92 a barrel, and analysts expect the prices to head lower in the coming year amid supply glut. The IEA's November report puts October supply at 105.4 mb/d and shows observed inventories rising 52 million barrels, the first build since June.
 
Mirae Asset Sharekhan said it expects Brent to end 2027 near $78.
 
4. Earnings growth strong
Elara Capital said that India’s resilient earnings trajectory has been instrumental in anchoring the downside for Indian equities. With earnings revisions gaining positive momentum, even a modest easing of external headwinds could set the stage for a market re-rating, it noted in a note recently.
 
Despite a weaker rupee, a Brent spike above $100/bbl, higher global yields and supply disruptions from the West Asia conflict, the Elara Universe posted robust sales/EBITDA/PAT growth of 23.8%/25.7%/28.7% YoY in Q2FY27. 
ALSO READ: India VIX up 9%, tops 17-mark; analysts say FII flows keep bulls in control
 
5. Technical outlook
Commenting on the technical outlook, SBI Securities said that for Nifty 50, the zone of 25400-25420 will act as a crucial support for the index, while the resistance lies in the zone of 25,710-25,730.
 
In the event of a surge above 25,730, the index can experience an extension of the rally towards 25,800, it opined. On the downside, if the index slips below the level of 25,400, then the next support is placed in the zone of 25,230-25,250. 
ALSO READ: Gold, silver prices fall amid stronger dollar, hawkish Fed signals

data.title: Contra funds get NFO boost: Is it time to bet against the market consensus?
data.description:
The contra fund category recorded net inflows of ₹1,694.13 crore in October 2026, compared with net outflows of ₹97.88 crore in September. At first glance, this may suggest rising investor interest. A closer look at the numbers, however, presents a more nuanced picture.
 
Around 88 per cent of the total inflows in October came from the new fund offer (NFO) of ICICI Prudential Contra Fund alone. This raises the question of whether investors are genuinely moving towards stocks and sectors that are currently out of favour with the market, or whether the surge in contra fund inflows is largely the result of one large NFO.
 
 
ICICI Prudential Contra Fund raised ₹1,488 crore through its NFO in October. This accounted for around 39 per cent of the total amount raised by all new schemes during the month. The other five schemes in the six-fund contra category together attracted net inflows of just ₹206 crore. This indicates that the October surge was not broad-based across the category.

Investors look for value beyond expensive stocks

Some investors are beginning to look beyond popular stocks and explore opportunities in companies and sectors that are currently out of favour. However, the shift remains limited.
 
A K Nigam, chief executive officer and director at BPN Fincap, said most retail investors were still chasing popular stocks. “Smallcap funds alone attracted ₹6,408 crore in October. However, a section of investors is now becoming wary of buying stocks at high valuations,” he said.
 
Nigam said that after two years of strong gains in midcap and smallcap stocks, shares of several companies were trading at price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios of more than 30 times. Investors were, therefore, looking for opportunities in relatively less-favoured sectors such as public-sector undertakings (PSUs), pharmaceuticals, fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) and banking.
 
Gurmeet Singh Chawla, managing director at Master Portfolio Services, said some investors were now looking at companies whose valuations had corrected. However, this did not mean the phase of momentum investing was over.
 
He cautioned that a stock being out of favour did not necessarily make it cheap. Investors should assess whether the company’s earnings could recover, whether its competitive position remained strong, and whether the underlying business fundamentals were sound.

Rising inflows: Confidence or NFO effect?

Nigam believes the return of inflows into contra funds reflects not just the launch of a new scheme but also some improvement in investor confidence. He said inflows into value-oriented funds had also increased, suggesting that some existing investors might have raised their exposure through systematic investment plans (SIPs) and lump-sum investments.
 
Chawla, however, said the rise in October inflows could have been driven mainly by the launch of the new scheme rather than a broadbased return of investor confidence.
 
With ₹1,488 crore coming from a single NFO, the contribution from existing schemes remained relatively modest. He said investors would need to track fresh inflows into existing schemes and SIP contributions over the coming months to determine whether interest in contra funds was genuinely increasing.

Why does a contra strategy matter in the current market?

Contra funds invest in companies and sectors that are currently out of favour with the market but have the potential to recover over time. Fund managers look for businesses whose market valuations do not adequately reflect their underlying operating strength and fundamentals.
 
Nigam said the strategy was relevant in the current market because valuations in some parts of the market had become expensive. Largecap stocks were trading at around 19 times earnings, while midcap and smallcap stocks were at around 27 times and 33 times, respectively, he said.
 
He also pointed to foreign institutional investor (FII) selling of ₹34,843 crore in October, which he said could create opportunities in good-quality companies.
 
According to Nigam, sectors such as information technology, pharmaceuticals, FMCG and banking could also offer opportunities if company fundamentals remained strong despite weak market sentiment.
 
Chawla also said contra strategies remained relevant, but urged caution. Not every beaten-down stock is worth investing in, he said. Some companies remain cheap because of weakening market share, poor balance sheets or weak business models.

How long should investors stay invested?

Contra investing requires patience because it can take years for the market to recognise the true potential of an overlooked company.
 
Nigam recommends an investment horizon of at least five years and, for better results, up to seven years. The first one or two years can be difficult, he said, as fund managers invest in stocks that are out of favour and the fund may underperform its benchmark.
 
Over the next three to five years, however, business conditions could improve and stock valuations could rise through a rerating.
 
Chawla also recommended an investment horizon of at least five to seven years. Improvements in earnings, changes in industry conditions and shifts in market sentiment can take time, he said.
 
Investors who cannot tolerate prolonged periods of underperformance may find it difficult to remain invested in such a strategy.

What should existing investors do?

Existing investors should not take decisions based solely on one month’s flow data.
 
Nigam advised investors against redeeming in panic. Those who invested in contra funds one or two years ago and were currently seeing weak performance could continue their SIPs if the fund’s strategy and portfolio remained aligned with their financial goals.
 
Investors who have stayed invested for four or five years and earned good returns could also continue holding. However, if contra funds have grown to more than 20 per cent of their overall portfolio, they may consider booking some profits.
 
Nigam cautioned investors against committing fresh money aggressively merely because inflows into the category had increased.
 
Chawla also said SIPs could continue if the fund’s portfolio and strategy remained consistent with the investor’s financial goals. However, any additional investment should be based on stock valuations, earnings prospects and the quality of the underlying businesses.
 
Investors should also examine how much their contra fund portfolio overlaps with their other equity funds. If the same stocks have high weights across funds, the diversification benefit may be limited.

How much should contra funds account for in a portfolio?

Nigam suggested allocating 10-15 per cent of an equity portfolio to contra funds. For investors with a long investment horizon and greater risk tolerance, the allocation could go up to a maximum of 20 per cent.
 
Chawla took a more conservative view, suggesting that contra funds account for around 5-10 per cent of the equity portfolio. This, he said, could allow investors to benefit from the strategy without creating excessive concentration risk.
Disclaimer: Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks. Investors should conduct their own due diligence or consult an advisor before making any investment decision.

data.title: Cauvery dispute: SC dismisses Tamil Nadu's pleas for 11 TMC water release
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed two pleas of the Tamil Nadu government seeking a direction to Karnataka for the release of 11 thousand million cubic (TMC) feet of Cauvery river water.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh said that Tamil Nadu has filed a third application for bringing on record some additional documents, which will also be dismissed.

In its pleas, the Tamil Nadu government sought directions to Karnataka to make sure that the backlog of 11 TMC of Cauvery water as on October 7 is cleared immediately and ensure the same at the rate of 1.3 TMC per day in 10 days at Billigundulu, a key water-measuring station on the banks of the river along the Karnataka-Tamil Nadu border.

 

On October 12, the top court reserved its decision on the two applications of the Tamil Nadu government.

The Karnataka government had told the top court that it would be difficult to meet Tamil Nadu's demand for the release of 11 TMC feet of Cauvery river water for making good a "shortfall" as this was a rain-deficit year and several areas have been declared drought-affected.

The Tamil Nadu government said it is only seeking its legitimate pro-rata share in the flows realised during the distress period, together with the backlog due to it, and the entire burden of meteorological and hydrological distress cannot be passed on to the lower riparian state, while Karnataka continues to utilise the available storage and inflows for irrigation and other requirements.

During the hearing, counsel for the Karnataka government submitted that this has been a very difficult year and several areas have been declared drought-hit.

"We have to ensure conservation of water so that the drinking water supply in residential areas is not affected," he had said, adding that Tamil Nadu has the benefit of the northeast monsoon in November, when its reservoirs will be replenished, while it will not help Karnataka.

"Every distress year, this has been the problem," he had said, adding that there has been proper application of mind by the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) at its 59th meeting held on October 8, in which it directed Karnataka to release 3,000 cusecs of Cauvery water at Billigundulu from October 9 for the next 15 days.

The counsel for the Tamil Nadu government had contended that Karnataka be directed to release the shortfall on a pro-rata basis, else crops in the state would be affected this year.

He said they cannot wait for another year as farmers in Tamil Nadu are facing a tough time and urged the court to at least make some interim arrangements.

In its plea filed through standing counsel B Karunakaran, the Tamil Nadu government said that, at a meeting held on September 24, the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC), based on the percentage of deficit, found that the flow realised at Billigundulu should have been 52.935 TMC and that there is a shortfall in the realisation of flows.

"In spite of noting the said deficit, the CWRC did not take any decision with regard to directing Karnataka to make good the shortfall and proceeded to reduce the flows from 6,000 cusecs to 4,000 cusecs. The CWRC directed Karnataka to ensure releases from its reservoirs so that 4,000 cusecs are received at Billigundulu in the next 15 days (effective September 24)," it said.

Giving the data of water release, the Tamil Nadu government said that even then, Karnataka did not adhere to the CWRC's directions and failed to ensure 4,000 cusecs every day.

It pointed out that Tamil Nadu's share in this distress year has to be decided on a pro-rata basis, but the CWMA, even after eight years since its constitution, has failed to formulate the distress formula -- a formula to share water during distress years, without any ambiguity or unfair treatment to a particular state.

It said the water directed to be released by the CWMA -- 4,000 cusecs at Billigundulu for 15 days starting September 24 and 3,000 cusecs from October 9 -- is grossly inadequate and does not redress the substantial backlog already accumulated.

The Tamil Nadu government said on October 8, the CWRC did not take any decision with regard to directing Karnataka to make good the shortfall and proceeded to reduce the flows from 4,000 cusecs to 3,000 cusecs effective October 9.

It sought directions to the Karnataka government to ensure and implement the CWMA's decision dated September 24 and make good the shortfall of 0.94 TMC towards the non-supply of water for the period from September 24 to October 7, and further flows as directed by the CWMA in its minutes dated October 8.

On September 24, the court asked the Karnataka government to respond to Tamil Nadu's plea seeking the release of its share of Cauvery water, alleging a shortfall in supply.

While the Tamil Nadu government told the court that it has already lost an early Kharif crop due to the lack of water, Karnataka said it is facing a "terrible drought situation".

The Tamil Nadu government approached the apex court on August 3, seeking directions to Karnataka for the immediate release of the water.

In its plea, Tamil Nadu has claimed that the quantum allocated to it by the CWRC as well as that released by its neighbour, Karnataka, is very little.

data.title: India's energy demand to grow 3 times faster than global average: IEA
data.description:
The West Asia conflict has exposed vulnerabilities in global energy supply chains, with disruptions to key shipping routes raising concerns about the availability and cost of oil and gas. The International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 examines how the duration of the crisis could shape global energy markets and influence countries' energy strategies.
 
The report also highlights India's growing energy needs, projecting that the country will account for more growth in energy demand over the next decade than any other country or region. Meeting this demand while ensuring reliable and affordable supplies will be a key challenge as India seeks to diversify its energy mix and reduce its exposure to external disruptions.
 
 

West Asia crisis shakes global energy markets

 
The scale of the disruption is reflected in the cumulative loss of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas from the Gulf since the crisis began, according to the IEA. By November 2026, the disruption to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz was still continuing, with the impact increasingly being passed on to consumers through higher prices as supply buffers ran down.
 
The pressure has been particularly severe in Asia, which accounted for around 80 per cent of the oil and nearly 90 per cent of the liquefied natural gas (LNG) that passed through the Strait before the crisis. Diesel supplies have also come under significant pressure, with prices crossing $200 per barrel.
 
The crisis is also prompting Gulf producers to reconsider their dependence on the Strait. According to the IEA, countries in the region are constructing or considering alternative pipeline projects with a combined capacity of around 7 million barrels per day. These projects could require investments of about $40 billion and add around $2 per barrel to export costs.
 
The IEA expects the disruption to have lasting implications for global energy trade, with countries increasingly looking to diversify suppliers, transport routes and energy sources. Solar power and nuclear energy could benefit from this shift, while faster electrification is emerging as another way to reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets.
 
For India, these changes carry particular significance. As one of the world's largest energy consumers and importers, the country faces the dual challenge of securing supplies amid geopolitical uncertainty and meeting rapidly rising domestic demand.
 

India's energy demand to surge

 
India is expected to record more growth in energy demand over the next decade than any other country or region, according to the IEA. The country's energy consumption is projected to grow by 2.5 per cent annually until 2035 under the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), around three times the global rate.
 
The increase will be driven by rising incomes, urbanisation, industrial expansion and growing demand for cooling and mobility. The IEA estimates that India will:
 
  • Add more than 12,000 cars to its roads every day over the next decade
  • See a 33 per cent increase in built-up spaces
  • Install an additional 200 million air conditioners in homes
  • Expand production of energy-intensive materials such as iron, steel and cement
 
This growth will put additional pressure on India's energy infrastructure and increase the need for reliable and affordable supplies.
 
However, India's dependence on imported fuels makes it particularly vulnerable to global disruptions. The country imports around 40 per cent of its overall energy requirements, including 90 per cent of its crude oil and 50 per cent of its natural gas.
 
The recent disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has highlighted this exposure, particularly for cooking gas. Around half of the LPG cylinders used by Indian households depend on supplies passing through the strategic waterway. LPG imports fell by more than 50 per cent during the first two months of the conflict, prompting the government to maximise domestic production and prioritise household supplies.
 

India's energy mix gets greener

 
Despite its growing energy requirements, India is making progress in diversifying its energy mix. Solar power accounted for half of the country's power capacity additions over the past decade, while India achieved its target of having 50 per cent of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
 
The IEA expects electricity demand to grow by 6 per cent annually over the next decade as transport, buildings and industries increasingly shift towards electricity.
 
Under the STEPS, India's electricity generation is projected to increase from 2,114 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 3,585 TWh by 2035. The share of non-fossil sources, including renewables and nuclear power, is expected to rise from around 28 per cent to 51 per cent over the same period.
 
However, coal will continue to play an important role in India's energy system because of its substantial domestic reserves. The IEA expects coal to increasingly provide flexibility to the power system as renewable energy capacity expands.
 

Dependence on imported fuels

 
India had nearly 6 million barrels per day (mb/d) of refining capacity in 2025, making it the world's fourth-largest country by refining capacity and third-largest by refinery runs. It is also the second-largest net crude oil importer after China.
 
With another 840,000 barrels per day of refining capacity under construction, India is expected to strengthen its role as an exporter of petroleum products, particularly diesel and other middle distillates.
 
However, the IEA projects that domestic crude oil production will decline by nearly 20 per cent by 2035 under the STEPS, while refining capacity expands by one million barrels per day. This will increase the country's overall crude import requirements, even as imports from West Asia remain broadly stable.
 
Cooking gas presents another challenge. India is the world's second-largest LPG importer, with domestic production meeting around 40 per cent of demand in 2025.
 
Under the STEPS, LPG demand is expected to grow by almost 400,000 barrels per day by 2035, while domestic supply increases by less than 100,000 barrels per day. Consequently, LPG imports could rise to nearly 1 million barrels per day.
 
The IEA also highlights a potential trade-off for refiners, as increasing LPG production could come at the expense of higher-value products such as diesel and petrol.
 

A faster shift to clean energy

 
The IEA's Additional Response Case (ARC) examines how faster adoption of clean energy, efficiency measures and domestic resources could reduce India's exposure to imported fuels.
 
Under this scenario, electric cars are adopted 30 per cent faster by 2035 than under the STEPS, while electrification and energy efficiency in industry accelerate. India could reduce its oil requirements by 580,000 barrels per day and natural gas consumption by 8 per cent compared with the STEPS by 2035.
 
This would also help bring LPG imports below 750,000 barrels per day, compared with nearly 1 million barrels per day under the STEPS.
 
The report suggests that faster electrification, greater use of renewables and improved energy efficiency could bring India closer to its ambition of achieving energy independence by 2047. However, the transition will require substantial investment in electricity infrastructure, domestic energy production and supply-chain diversification.

data.title: Brent seen at $75-85 in 2027 as oil surplus builds: Mirae Asset Sharekhan
data.description:
Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion. Oil has spent November unwinding the fear it priced in during October. Brent has fallen nearly 19 per cent, from around $118 a barrel in late October to $95, and both Brent and WTI have corrected 15 per cent in a month while still up 50 per cent for the year. In the physical market, Dated Brent, which traded $25-30 a barrel above futures at the end of October, now trades less than a dollar away. The Republican defeat in the US midterms eased fears of a wider US-Iran war, and much of the geopolitical premium went with it. On Thursday, reports that President Trump is weighing further strikes on Iran lifted prices only until the US, China and Russia agreed to boost production and supply of refined products. A market that shrugs off war headlines has stopped paying for scarcity.
 
 
Refining economics have deflated alongside crude. The benchmark 3-2-1 crack spread has corrected 22 per cent in a month, US gasoline has eased to $3.82 a gallon and diesel has slipped below $6. Yet gasoline is still 24 per cent more expensive than a year ago and diesel nearly 60 per cent higher. Global crude processing capacity was still down 2.5 per cent at the end of the third quarter, and Ukrainian drone attacks on 13 Russian refineries since November began have cut Russian runs to 4.2 million barrels a day (mb/d) from 5 mb/d in late October. Crude can be plentiful while diesel and jet fuel stay scarce.
 
Iran has stepped up attacks on Hormuz shipping and struck US facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while Saudi Arabia faces daily Houthi drone and missile attacks. The International Energy Agency (IEA) puts October Gulf oil exports excluding Oman at 18.4 mb/d, still about 26 per cent below pre-war, with crude flows back to 15 mb/d, roughly 82 per cent of pre-war volumes in October but have once again receded to 8-9mbpd. Saudi crude production rose 970,000 b/d to 9.2 mb/d, up from a 36-year low in August; Iraq is pumping at a seven-year high and Kirkuk–Ceyhan is flowing again. The mix is changing: in early November, Gulf crude exports excluding Iran ran about 2.0 mb/d below October, while refined-product exports climbed to about 65 per cent of pre-war levels. Gulf-to-China supertanker rates are down almost a quarter from October's record.
 The IEA's November report puts October supply at 105.4 mb/d and shows observed inventories rising 52 million barrels, the first build since June. It expects fourth-quarter supply of about 105 mb/d to exceed demand by roughly 1.7 mb/d, sees 2026 demand falling 2.7 mb/d to 102.3 mb/d, and projects a larger surplus in 2027. That assumes Gulf exports stay 26 per cent below pre-war; meanwhile. OPEC's October crude output rose 930,000 b/d to an eight-month high of 22.8 mb/d, and OPEC+ production of about 41.23 mb/d is near pre-war levels.
 
Asia shows both sides of the trade. China's refining system, the world's largest at roughly 18–19m b/d, is running below 80 per cent of capacity, with independents at just 56 per cent, and Chinese gasoline and diesel demand is forecast to fall about 9.5 per cent this year as EVs and LNG trucks spread. Beijing is exporting the surplus: it added 5.68m tonnes of export quota, and November export plans are up 25 per cent, with gasoline doubling. India is the mirror image. October consumption rose 2.7 per cent year on year to 20.494 million tonnes, the highest for the month, led by a 12.0 per cent jump in diesel. Yet India's crude basket has climbed from an average of $89 to $96, and elevated shipping and insurance costs weigh on the rupee, the deficits and inflation. China is exporting spare capacity.
 
US weekly data point the same way. As of 13 November, crude inventories were 3.6 per cent below the five-year seasonal average and gasoline 2.3 per cent above, but distillates were 7.0 per cent below. Crude production rose 0.1 per cent to a record high, and refinery utilisation was 92.8 per cent in the week to 23 October. Gasoline is comfortable; middle distillates are not, precisely where Russian outages and the capacity shortfall bite.
 
The surplus has yet to reach the tanks. Onshore inventories fell sharply (500mb) in 2026, remain below their five-year average, and have yet to be replenished. We therefore expect a smaller 2027 surplus than the IEA projects. Dated Brent should end 2027 near $78, within a $75-85 Brent range, with WTI in the mid-$70s to $80.
